record.context_brief: Typical paths producing large stationary delays
record.original_question: For the two-server queue regimes just described, namely the case rho = 1 with a subexponential service-time distribution and the case rho in (1, 2) with a heavy-tailed service-time distribution having all power moments finite, what are the typical sample paths that lead to large values of the stationary waiting time D?

evidence.quote: Again let D be the stationary waiting time. We formulate the following questions: what may the asymptotics for P(D > x) be when x is large and what is the typical sample path which lead to such a large value of the stationary waiting time.
It would be great to understand what are in these cases the typical paths which lead to large values of D.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a FCFS GI/GI/2 queue with two identical servers. Jobs arrive at epochs of a renewal process with i.i.d. interarrival times having mean 1/λ, and require i.i.d. service times {σ_n} (independent of the arrivals) with common distribution F on [0,∞) and mean Eσ. Define the traffic intensity ρ = λ Eσ/2 across the two servers (so the per-server load is ρ). Assume the queue is stable and let D denote the stationary waiting time (the steady-state delay before a typical arriving customer's service begins).

Determine, in each of the following two regimes, the structure of the "typical" sample paths of the input that produce a large value of D, in the sense of describing the conditional behavior of the interarrival and service-time sequences (e.g. how many service times become atypically large, of which order, and on what time scale relative to x) given the rare event {D > x}, as x → ∞:

(a) The critically loaded case ρ = 1 with the integrated-tail (residual) service distribution F^I subexponential.

(b) The overloaded case ρ ∈ (1,2) with service-time distribution F heavy-tailed but possessing all power moments E[σ^k] < ∞ for every k ≥ 1.

In each case, identify the most probable mechanism (number, sizes, and timing of "big jumps" in the service-time sequence, and any associated behavior of the arrival process) leading to {D > x}, and give the resulting asymptotics of P(D > x) as x → ∞.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work by Foss and Korshunov (and by Boxma, Foss et al.) developed a "principle of s−k big jumps" for GI/GI/s queues and obtained, for the half-loaded GI/GI/2 case (ρ=1) with intermediate regularly varying tails, sharp tail asymptotics for the stationary waiting time, identifying typical paths with one or two big service jumps depending on the variance. The case ρ ∈ (1,2) with service times having all moments finite (e.g. Weibull-type tails) is treated in later works on Weibullian multi-server queues, but a complete description of typical paths in full generality is not established. The status is therefore partially solved.

status_evidence.title: On Large Delays in Multi-Server Queues with Heavy Tails
status_evidence.snippet: Upper and lower bounds for the tail distribution of stationary waiting time in stable GI/GI/s FCFS queue; for intermediate regularly varying tails, principle of s−k big jumps gives the most probable way for waiting time to be large.
status_evidence.claim: Typical-path description (principle of big jumps) established in multi-server queues for certain heavy-tailed regimes.

status_evidence.title: Tail asymptotics for delay in a half-loaded GI/GI/2 queue with heavy-tailed job sizes
status_evidence.snippet: For ρ=1 two-server queue: with finite variance two effects (one extreme job vs two big jobs) dominate; with infinite variance only the single-big-jump effect dominates.
status_evidence.claim: Half-loaded GI/GI/2 case (ρ=1) typical-path structure has been characterized for several tail regimes.

status_evidence.title: Queue length asymptotics for the multiple-server queue with heavy-tailed Weibull service times
status_evidence.snippet: Tail asymptotics for multi-server queues with Weibull service times having all moments finite.
status_evidence.claim: Cases with all moments finite have been partially analyzed in subsequent literature.
